**MEMO — Internal Engineering**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** [Date]

Over the past quarter, our local inference hardware has become the subject of a recurring debate. Our GPU cluster is running hot during peak hours, batch queues are lengthening, and latency on interactive workloads has crept from the low hundreds of milliseconds toward something users notice. The obvious response is to buy more cards. The less obvious response — and the one I want to argue for — is that we should spend the next two months proving we actually need them.

Let me start with the economics, because they frame everything else. The hardware we're considering would cost roughly the equivalent of two full quarters of our operating budget, before power, cooling, and the engineering time to integrate and maintain it. That is not an unreasonable sum for a capability we genuinely need, but it is a large enough sum that we should be confident the need is real rather than an artifact of poor scheduling. Right now, our utilisation numbers tell an uncomfortable story: peak-hour saturation, yes, but average utilisation across the fleet sits somewhere in the thirties. That gap between peak and average is the signature of a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem. If we can flatten the peaks — by batching offline work into off-peak windows, prioritising interactive requests, and consolidating small jobs — we may recover a substantial fraction of the headroom we think we're missing, at a cost of a few engineer-weeks rather than a capital outlay.

Latency deserves its own consideration, because it's the strongest argument on the "buy" side. Interactive inference is latency-sensitive in a way batch work is not, and no amount of clever queueing will make a saturated card fast. If our p99 latency is degrading user experience today, that is a real cost being paid every day we wait. But I'd push back gently on how much of our latency problem is truly capacity-driven. Some of it, I suspect, is model placement (models being loaded and evicted repeatedly), some is network overhead between services, and some is simply that our request routing doesn't distinguish urgent from deferrable work. Those are cheap fixes with fast payback. If we fix them and latency still suffers at peak, we will have learned something precise about how much hardware we actually need — and we'll be buying it for the right reason.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy, which is genuinely valuable: today, the failure of a single node degrades our interactive capacity noticeably, and our maintenance windows are constrained by the fact that we have no slack. That is a legitimate argument for expansion, and I don't want to minimise it. But it's worth noting that better utilisation also improves reliability indirectly — a fleet with consolidated, well-scheduled workloads is easier to drain, patch, and fail over than one where capacity is scattered across half-idle nodes. And a capital purchase made hastily tends to lock in architectural decisions (rack layouts, power contracts, vendor relationships) that are expensive to unwind. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are almost entirely reversible. If we invest two months in scheduling and observability and it turns out we were wrong — that we truly are capacity-constrained — we've lost little except time, and we've gained a monitoring and orchestration layer we'd want anyway. If we buy hardware and it turns out we were wrong, we've lost a great deal more, and the sunk cost will exert a quiet gravitational pull on our future decisions.

This is really a question about opportunity cost. Every dollar and engineer-hour spent on new hardware is a dollar and hour not spent on product work, on the observability stack we keep deferring, or on the model-efficiency experiments (quantisation, distillation) that could shrink our footprint regardless of fleet size. The option value of waiting is high: hardware prices in this space have been falling in performance-per-dollar terms, and our demand picture will be clearer after the next product cycle. Buying now means paying today's prices for yesterday's uncertainty.

So my recommendation is this: commit to a two-month utilisation improvement effort, with explicit, pre-agreed thresholds. If, after that work, peak-hour utilisation still exceeds roughly 85 percent and p99 interactive latency remains above our target, we proceed with the hardware purchase — with a much sharper specification of what we need and why. I want to be honest about the uncertainty here: I may be underestimating our growth trajectory, and there's a scenario where deferring the purchase costs us a quarter of user-visible degradation. But the asymmetry of the two mistakes favours patience. Buying too early is expensive and hard to reverse; waiting too long, in the worst case, costs us some latency we can partially mitigate in the meantime.

I'd like the team's feedback by end of week, with a view to starting the utilisation work the following Monday.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Internal draft

Over the past quarter, our inference workloads have grown to the point where GPU utilisation has become a recurring topic in standup. The question in front of us is simple to state and harder to answer: do we purchase additional local hardware, or do we invest engineering time in raising the utilisation of the fleet we already own? I want to lay out the trade-offs as I see them and make a recommendation, with the caveat that several of the numbers below are estimates and I'll flag where I'm least confident.

The case for buying more hardware is the obvious one: it removes the constraint immediately. Our p99 inference latency has crept from roughly 180ms to 340ms during peak hours, and queueing during batch jobs occasionally delays downstream teams. New capacity would restore headroom overnight, and headroom has real value — it absorbs traffic spikes, lets us experiment without worrying about displacing production load, and reduces the operational risk that comes with running everything hot. There is also a reliability argument. A fleet running at 85–90% utilisation has no slack to survive a node failure gracefully; when one of our two larger boxes goes down for maintenance, the other one saturates and latency degrades for everyone. Spare capacity is, in a real sense, reliability you can measure.

But the case against buying is stronger than it first appears. Our average utilisation sits around 45%, which means we own roughly twice the compute we actually use on a time-weighted basis. That gap is not primarily a capacity problem; it's a scheduling and architecture problem. Batch inference jobs run on whatever hardware happens to be free rather than being packed against interactive traffic. Model weights are duplicated across nodes because we never invested in a shared serving layer. Several legacy workloads pin GPUs they barely use because nobody has revisited the allocation since the original owner left the team. Each of these is fixable, and the fixes are cheap relative to hardware. A well-understood GPU at this tier costs on the order of $30–40k, plus power, cooling, and the rack space we'd need to find. The engineering cost of a proper scheduler rollout and a serving consolidation effort is maybe two engineers for six to eight weeks — call it $60–80k of fully loaded time. If that work lifts utilisation from 45% to 70%, we've effectively added capacity equivalent to more than one new node at roughly half the cost, without adding a single watt to our power budget.

There's also the question of opportunity cost, and it cuts both ways. Money spent on hardware is money not spent on the serving layer, observability improvements, or the model-quality work several teams have been asking for. Conversely, engineering time spent on utilisation is time not spent on product features. I think the asymmetry favours the utilisation work, though, because the scheduler and serving-layer investments are durable — they pay off regardless of how much hardware we eventually own — whereas a new node is a point solution that depreciates and becomes obsolete on a three-to-four-year horizon.

Reversibility matters too. Hardware purchases are largely irreversible; once the capital is spent, we own the asset whether or not the demand materialises, and reselling used accelerators recovers only a fraction of cost. Utilisation work is the opposite: it's a sequence of small, individually reversible decisions. If the scheduler rollout stalls or the consolidation effort turns out to be more disruptive than expected, we can stop, and we've lost weeks rather than tens of thousands of dollars. That option value is worth something, especially given my main uncertainty: I am genuinely unsure whether our utilisation ceiling is 65% or 80%. If it's the former, the math gets tighter and we may still need hardware — but we'll know that in eight weeks rather than guessing now.

So my recommendation is this: defer the hardware purchase for one quarter. Fund a focused utilisation effort — scheduler improvements, serving consolidation, and an audit of stale allocations — with an explicit checkpoint at the end. If p99 latency is back under 250ms at peak and utilisation has moved meaningfully, we likely don't need the purchase at all. If it hasn't, we'll buy with much better evidence about what size and configuration we actually need, and the scheduling work will make the new hardware more effective anyway. The one thing I'd carve out immediately: if a genuine capacity emergency hits before the checkpoint — sustained saturation, or a second node failure — we escalate the purchase decision without waiting out the quarter.

I'd like to discuss this at Thursday's planning session. Comments welcome before then.

— Infra Working Group
